sections.title: People & Politics
sections.description: Important developments in governments, societies and the people shaping the world.

cards.title: Egyptian Editor Detained for Running Unlicensed Website
cards.content: The editor-in-chief of Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr, Lina Attalah, was detained for several hours after a court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website and ordered its closure. She was released after paying a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds. The verdict has been criticized by human rights groups and press freedom advocates, who see it as a blow to press freedom. Mada Masr had faced pressure from authorities over its journalism, and Attalah had faced years of harassment and intimidation. The site was a vital source of critical reporting in Egypt, but the court's decision has shut it down. Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars.

cards.title: Twin Brothers, American Woman Plead Guilty to Dating Scam
cards.content: Twin brothers from Ghana, Jamal and Kamal Abubakari, and American woman Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie have pleaded guilty to being part of an international criminal network that defrauded people on dating sites and social media. The group targeted elderly people in the US and Europe, using fake identities to lure them into believing they were in a romantic relationship, before persuading them to transfer large sums of money into bank accounts in Ghana. Between July 2024 and April 2026, the victims collectively lost $9 million. The three accused face up to 20 years in jail and will be sentenced next year. As part of the plea, they agreed to forfeit pieces of jewelry, including luxury watches and earrings, which were seized during their arrest. The case highlights a growing problem of elderly Americans being targeted by criminal networks operating in the US and West Africa.

cards.title: Zookeeper Killed by Persian Leopards at Dutch Zoo
cards.content: At a Dutch zoo called Beekse Bergen, a 40-year veteran zookeeper has sadly passed away. She was attacked by two Persian leopards in their enclosure on Saturday. The woman, who started her job at 17, was caring for the leopards when she was injured and taken to hospital. Despite her efforts to alert colleagues, she died due to her injuries. An investigation will be conducted into the incident, and the zoo has expressed its condolences to the woman's family and friends. The leopards, which were brought inside due to bad weather, will not be euthanized and are being treated as normal predators. The zoo will create a memorial for staff and visitors to pay their respects.

sections.title: Science and technology
sections.description: Discover breakthroughs in science, space, computing and emerging technology.

cards.title: Denisovans' First Confirmed Radius Found in China Cave
cards.content: Scientists have discovered the first confirmed Denisovan radius, a forearm bone, in a cave in southwest China. The radius combines features of Neanderthals and modern humans, but its owner is identified as Denisovan through preserved proteins. This discovery fills a long-standing gap in the group's known distribution in the region and provides rare clues to their physical traits and adaptations. The team used a combination of morphological analysis and ZooMS, a technique that examines protein signatures, to identify the radius and four other Denisovan remains from the Bianfu Cave. The findings were published in Nature and suggest that Denisovans may have thrived in a region with a relatively warm climate and abundant food resources during a glacial period.

cards.title: SK Hynix Reports Record Profit with 327.9% Revenue Growth
cards.content: South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix has reported a record high quarterly profit, surpassing estimates, with revenue rising 327.9% from last year and operating profit climbing 632.1%. The company also announced plans to return over $25 billion to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. SK Hynix expects its new high-bandwidth memory technology, HBM4, to surpass its previous generation in the fourth quarter, with 14 major customers securing long-term agreements for over 50% of its production capacity for 2027 and 2028. The company plans to significantly increase investment next year and expects memory demand to outpace supply through 2030. }

cards.title: Anthropic Reveals $131.7 Billion Cash Reserve
cards.content: A nearly six-year-old artificial intelligence lab, Anthropic, has disclosed having an astonishing $131.7 billion in cash and short-term investments as of June 30. This amount surpasses every non-bank U.S. company except for Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet. The company is set to go public, with reports suggesting it could raise over $100 billion, which would bring its cash hoard to over $230 billion. However, Anthropic's vast cash reserves are not a guarantee of its future, as it has significant commitments for computing power that will start to kick in over the next few years, with total estimated future lease obligations and commitments reaching over half a trillion.

sections.title: Health & wellness
sections.description: Medical research, public health and discoveries that affect everyday wellbeing.

cards.title: Blood test reveals dementia risk clues
cards.content: A large study of over 316,000 adults found that a routine blood test can reveal clues about future dementia risk. Researchers discovered that people with unusually low or high hemoglobin levels were more likely to develop dementia. The study suggests that hemoglobin levels may reflect broader aspects of physical health associated with brain aging. The findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also identified differences between Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia. The study's lead researcher emphasized that the results do not establish a direct causal relationship, but rather suggest that abnormal hemoglobin levels may be a visible marker of wider physical vulnerability relevant to brain health. The researchers suggest that existing blood test results could potentially help scientists investigate connections between general physical health and long-term cognitive decline.

cards.title: Antibodies linked to childhood cancer hinder DNA repair
cards.content: Researchers in Norway have found that antibodies associated with childhood cancer can enter cells and bind DNA repair proteins, suggesting a possible route by which the immune system could weaken genetic safeguards. The study, published in Frontiers in Immunology, analyzed blood samples from 175 adults and children with cancer and compared them to samples from healthy individuals. The results show that children with cancer had substantially more circulating IgG antibodies targeting DNA repair proteins than young adults or older individuals. The findings suggest that these antibodies can appear well before cancer develops and may interfere with DNA repair, potentially leading to cancer. The researchers propose that these antibodies entering a cell or its nucleus could attach to DNA repair proteins and prevent them from working normally, leading to increased cellular damage that could lead to cancer development.

sections.title: Environment
sections.description: Climate, oceans, ecosystems and the changing planet around us.

cards.title: Cyclone Arnab forms over Bay of Bengal, hits Andhra Pradesh coast
cards.content: A severe cyclonic storm named Cyclone Arnab has formed over the Bay of Bengal and is expected to make landfall on the Andhra Pradesh coast on October 28, bringing extremely heavy rainfall and strong winds to coastal areas. The cyclone's impact is also expected to affect Odisha, Telangana, and Chhattisgarh with heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, and strong winds. Meanwhile, a western disturbance is forecasted to bring rain, thunderstorms, and snowfall to parts of northern India. The India Meteorological Department reports that the cyclone is moving west-north-westwards and is expected to cross the Andhra Pradesh coast between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam on October 28.

cards.title: Antarctica Turns Green and Red Due to Penguin Droppings Fueling Algae
cards.content: Antarctica, known for its vast expanses of white ice and snow-covered mountains, is unexpectedly turning green and red in some areas. This phenomenon has caught the attention of scientists who are trying to understand the connection to climate change. One factor contributing to the colorful patches is penguin droppings, which provide nutrients to microscopic algae growing on the snow. The scientists suspect that this natural process may accelerate local melting, adding to the effects of a warming climate. The impact of penguin droppings on the melting of Antarctica's snow is still being studied, and the effects are not yet fully understood.

cards.title: Srinagar's Water Crisis Worsens due to Climate Change
cards.content: In Srinagar, a water crisis has been ongoing for years, causing daily struggles for residents like Mehak and Zamrood. The absence of a regular water supply has led to the installation of tanks and a hand pump at their homes. Climate change is affecting Doodh Ganga, a vital source of drinking water, causing erratic water supply, low flow, and dry taps. The river's water availability is decreasing due to rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and declining snowmelt. The Kashmir Valley's 24 watersheds, including Doodh Ganga, are experiencing similar impacts.

sections.title: Entertainment
sections.description: Stories from film, music, sports, culture and the world of entertainment.

cards.title: Meghan Joins Junior MasterChef Australia as Co-Host
cards.content: The Duchess of Sussex, Meghan, has been confirmed as a co-host for the new season of Junior MasterChef Australia, joining Poh Ling Yeow. This comes after Meghan appeared as a guest judge on MasterChef Australia last year, which drew its largest Sunday audience since 2023. Meghan's return to Australia follows a four-day tour she undertook with Prince Harry in April, which included an announcement about her MasterChef debut. Meghan said she is excited to participate in the show, sharing her love of cooking with her own kids. This new role comes as Meghan faces increased scrutiny over allegations against her father, Thomas Markle, which he denies. The Sussexes announced they were moving back to the UK from California in August, after stepping back from their royal duties in 2020 to pursue media careers.

cards.title: Spotify Corrects Error in Welsh Version of Dolly Parton's Jolene
cards.content: A Welsh version of Dolly Parton's hit song Jolene, featuring Bronwen Lewis and Jada Star, was mistakenly uploaded to Spotify with Irish lyrics. The song, recorded before Parton's death, features parts in English and Welsh, but the lyrics on Spotify showed it as Irish. After the BBC approached Spotify for comment, the error was removed. This is the second posthumous release from Parton, who was of Welsh descent and won 10 Grammy awards. Jolene, released in 1973, is about the fear of losing her husband to another woman, and it has had over one billion streams on Spotify. The Welsh version of the song was translated by Lewis and recorded with Parton's niece Star, and it follows Parton's revelation of her Welsh ancestry during a 2008 concert in Cardiff.

cards.title: Marzamemi Festival Applies to Hold Family-Friendly Event on Richmond Green
cards.content: A family-friendly Italian-themed festival, the Marzamemi Festival, has applied to hold a three-day event on Richmond Green in south-west London in June. The event, which features live music, food, and activities for children, has received some support but also 45 objections from residents who are concerned about noise and restricted access to the park. The Richmond Society has objected to the event, citing concerns that it will take away public access to a large area of the green, potentially constituting a public nuisance. The event's founder, Emily Ceraudo, describes it as a 'boutique, family-friendly celebration' that aims to support local businesses. The Richmond Council's licensing committee will make a decision on the event in the coming days.

sections.title: economy
sections.description: Markets, businesses, trade and economic changes shaping the global economy.

cards.title: White House Tries to Bridge Economic Data Gap with Voters' Perceptions
cards.content: The White House is facing a familiar dilemma, where economic numbers aren't necessarily bad, but the public mood is. The issue is the disconnect between the solid economic data, such as low unemployment and strong growth, and the high prices that voters are paying at supermarkets and gas stations. President Donald Trump has promised to bring prices down, but the latest inflation report confirms that prices remain high. Trump's administration has tried to shift the focus from prices to economic indicators like GDP and the stock market, but voters are judging the economy by what they pay at the supermarket and whether they can keep up with bills. The challenge for Trump is to bridge the gap between the economic data and the public's perception of the economy. His predecessor, Joe Biden, faced a similar challenge during the 2024 election campaign, but ultimately failed to convince voters that the economy was working for them.

cards.title: Naomi Nomi Revolutionizes Fashion with Quality, Long-Lasting Clothing
cards.content: Naomi Mishkin, the founder of Naomi Nomi, is revolutionizing the fashion industry by producing high-quality, long-lasting clothing at a higher price point. The average customer starts with one shirt and returns for three more within six months, as they realize the value of her products. Mishkin's approach is a departure from the fast fashion industry, which has mastered the art of cutting production costs to the bone. She uses cotton and wool, making her shirts pricier than fast fashion, but lasting longer. Naomi Nomi's success is attributed to the growing backlash against companies that prioritize profit over quality and the environment. The fashion industry has undergone significant changes over the past few decades, with a shift towards planned obsolescence and the use of cheaper materials. However, some consumers are now looking for brands that offer quality, durability, and sustainability, and Naomi Nomi is capitalizing on this trend.

cards.title: Nscale to Build UK's Largest AI Data Centre in Loughton, Despite Microsoft Pullout
cards.content: Nscale, a tech company, has reaffirmed its plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre in Loughton, Essex, despite Microsoft's decision to pull out of the project. Microsoft had agreed to fund a supercomputer at the site, but its involvement has been terminated. Nscale is exploring alternative power sources and maintaining a strong relationship with Microsoft for other projects globally. The data centre was expected to receive its power supply by the end of this year, but this has been delayed until the 2030s due to a London-wide grid issue. The project is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it opens.
